verses.text: Belshazzar the king made a great feast to a thousand of his lords, and drank wine before the thousand.

Belshazzar, while he tasted the wine, commanded to bring the golden and silver vessels which Nebuchadnezzar his father had taken out of the temple which was in Jerusalem; that the king and his lords, his wives and his concubines, might drink from them.
Then they brought the golden vessels that were taken out of the temple of God’s house which was at Jerusalem; and the king and his lords, his wives and his concubines, drank from them.
They drank wine, and praised the gods of gold, and of silver, of brass, of iron, of wood, and of stone.
In the same hour, the fingers of a man’s hand came out and wrote near the lamp stand on the plaster of the wall of the king’s palace. The king saw the part of the hand that wrote.
Then the king’s face was changed in him, and his thoughts troubled him; and the joints of his thighs were loosened, and his knees struck one against another.

The king cried aloud to bring in the enchanters, the Chaldeans, and the soothsayers. The king spoke and said to the wise men of Babylon, Whoever shall read this writing, and show me its interpretation, shall be clothed with purple, and have a chain of gold about his neck, and shall be the third ruler in the kingdom.
Then came in all the king’s wise men; but they could not read the writing, nor make known to the king the interpretation.
Then was king Belshazzar greatly troubled, and his face was changed in him, and his lords were perplexed.

The queen by reason of the words of the king and his lords came into the banquet house: the queen spoke and said, O king, live forever; don’t let your thoughts trouble you, nor let your face be changed.

There is a man in your kingdom, in whom is the spirit of the holy gods; and in the days of your father light and understanding and wisdom, like the wisdom of the gods, were found in him; and the king Nebuchadnezzar your father, the king, your father, made him master of the magicians, enchanters, Chaldeans, and soothsayers;

because an excellent spirit, and knowledge, and understanding, interpreting of dreams, and showing of dark sentences, and dissolving of doubts, were found in the same Daniel, whom the king named Belteshazzar. Now let Daniel be called, and he will show the interpretation.
Then was Daniel brought in before the king. The king spoke and said to Daniel, Are you that Daniel, who are of the children of the captivity of Judah, whom the king my father brought out of Judah?
I have heard of you, that the spirit of the gods is in you, and that light and understanding and excellent wisdom are found in you.
Now the wise men, the enchanters, have been brought in before me, that they should read this writing, and make known to me its interpretation; but they could not show the interpretation of the thing.

But I have heard of you, that you can give interpretations, and dissolve doubts; now if you can read the writing, and make known to me its interpretation, you shall be clothed with purple, and have a chain of gold about your neck, and shall be the third ruler in the kingdom.
Then Daniel answered before the king, Let your gifts be to yourself, and give your rewards to another; nevertheless I will read the writing to the king, and make known to him the interpretation.
You, king, the Most High God gave Nebuchadnezzar your father the kingdom, and greatness, and glory, and majesty:

and because of the greatness that he gave him, all the peoples, nations, and languages trembled and feared before him: whom he would he killed, and whom he would he kept alive; and whom he would he raised up, and whom he would he put down.
But when his heart was lifted up, and his spirit was hardened so that he dealt proudly, he was deposed from his kingly throne, and they took his glory from him:

and he was driven from the sons of men, and his heart was made like the animals’, and his dwelling was with the wild donkeys; he was fed with grass like oxen, and his body was wet with the dew of the sky; until he knew that the Most High God rules in the kingdom of men, and that he sets up over it whomever he will.
You, his son, Belshazzar, have not humbled your heart, though you knew all this,

but have lifted up yourself against the Lord of heaven; and they have brought the vessels of his house before you, and you and your lords, your wives and your concubines, have drunk wine from them; and you have praised the gods of silver and gold, of brass, iron, wood, and stone, which don’t see, nor hear, nor know; and the God in whose hand your breath is, and whose are all your ways, you have not glorified.
Then was the part of the hand sent from before him, and this writing was inscribed.
This is the writing that was inscribed: MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN.
This is the interpretation of the thing: MENE; God has counted your kingdom, and brought it to an end;
TEKEL; you are weighed in the balances, and are found wanting.
PERES; your kingdom is divided, and given to the Medes and Persians.
Then commanded Belshazzar, and they clothed Daniel with purple, and put a chain of gold about his neck, and made proclamation concerning him, that he should be the third ruler in the kingdom.
In that night Belshazzar the Chaldean King was slain.
Darius the Mede received the kingdom, being about sixty-two years old.

footnotes.content: A thousand lords at one feast—what a show of power and pleasure. Notice how the chapter opens not with what's broken, but with what looks most secure: wine, company, the king's command over all of it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Belshazzar commands them to bring the sacred vessels from Jerusalem's temple—gold and silver looted by his grandfather. Desecration feels like freedom to a king who's forgotten who really holds the throne.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They drank from holy cups as if they were common cups. There's a kind of blindness that comes when we treat sacred things as our own playthings—we stop seeing the hand that made them at all.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After drinking from God's vessels, they praised idols—silver, wood, stone. It's the old lie: make something with your own hands and call it god. The real God has always preferred a humble heart to a decorated wall.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Then a hand appears—just the fingers. No arm, no voice, just writing. The Lord speaks sometimes in the smallest ways, and the king is frozen. Pride quiets fast when God shows up.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His face changes, his bones shake loose, his knees knock together. Fear grips a man fast when he knows something sacred has entered the room and he knows he's not ready.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king calls for the wise men and promises rewards—purple, gold, high rank. He's still trying to fix this with the tools he knows: money, honor, power. But this is not that kind of problem.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All his wise men gather and all of them fail. When judgment comes from the Living God, the world's learned men are like children staring at words they'll never understand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now Belshazzar is not just troubled—he's 'greatly troubled.' His lords are perplexed. Pride has left them. What's left is just a room full of men who know something is terribly wrong.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The queen remembers something—there was a man, in your father's days. Even in a pagan court, a woman kept the memory of something true. She speaks calmly: there's help here, if you'll listen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She describes Daniel: a man in whom the spirit of the holy gods rested—light, understanding, wisdom. Even foreign rulers knew when a man carried something deeper than learning.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Daniel had an 'excellent spirit'—the queen remembers him solving riddles, reading dark things. Some people you don't forget, even after years apart. They leave a mark on the memory.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king asks Daniel: Are you that one brought from Judah? Notice—he's calling a captive by the only name he can anchor to: where he came from. But captives are the Lord's people too.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Belshazzar has heard the news about Daniel's wisdom and light. A man's faithfulness travels before him even in exile, even in a foreign court. Character leaves traces.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king admits: my wise men couldn't read it, couldn't say what it means. Now he's asking a captive from Jerusalem for help. Pride and panic make strange partners.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Again the king offers: purple, gold, the third place in the kingdom. He doesn't yet know that Daniel's heart is anchored somewhere else—somewhere no earthly reward can touch.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Daniel refuses the gifts and says simply: I will read it anyway. This is the stance of a man who serves a higher King—free to speak truth because he's not buying it back with reward.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Daniel begins his interpretation by reminding the king: Your father Nebuchadnezzar held his kingdom by the grace of the Most High God. Even great power is borrowed power, held at God's pleasure.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Before Nebuchadnezzar, peoples trembled and feared. He killed whom he wished, saved whom he wished. That's what unchecked power looks like. And the Lord watched every choice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But his heart lifted up. His spirit hardened. He dealt proudly—and was deposed. This is the pattern: God resists the proud. A king who forgets who sits higher than kings falls fast.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nebuchadnezzar was driven from men and his mind became like beasts'—grass, dew, wild donkeys. A humbling so deep it was like death, until he finally knew: the Most High God rules, and sets up whomever He will.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: And you, Belshazzar—you knew all this. You'd seen your father brought low, raised up again through brokenness. Yet you didn't humble your heart. Knowing the truth and living it are not the same thing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Instead you lifted yourself against the Lord of heaven. You took His holy cups, praised dead idols, and forgot the God in whose hand your very breath lives. That's when the hand came.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The hand was sent from before Him. Each letter traced on the wall was mercy dressed as judgment—a final call, written in stone and plaster where a king could not miss it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN—four words in Aramaic, counting words that carry the weight of a kingdom's end. Each syllable a judgment; each letter a door closing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: MENE means numbered—your days are counted, your kingdom finished. God doesn't rage; He simply says: it's done. Finality can come quietly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: TEKEL: you are weighed in the balances and found wanting. Not heavier than yesterday, but lighter than what goodness demands. One verse: a king's entire worth, measured and found short.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: PERES: your kingdom is divided and given to Medes and Persians. What you hold so tightly will be taken and given to strangers. Pride's greatest fear is irrelevance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: That night, Belshazzar dresses Daniel in purple and gives him the third place anyway. One last gesture of a dying king. But rewards can't save. Nothing can, now.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In that night Belshazzar was slain. The writing came at evening; the king fell before morning. God works fast when the hour comes. The feast ended in silence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Darius the Mede received the kingdom, being sixty-two years old. Readers today hear an echo in this quiet transfer of power—how God's plans don't stall for human pride, how He raises up those He's chosen, how empires turn without ceasing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
